chunks: "Process corners are a way of bounding manufacturing variation.
In a real fab, transistors from different wafers and lots come out faster or slower than typical: threshold voltage, gate length, oxide thickness and so on drift.
The foundry characterizes this and provides model files for extreme-but-realistic cases, usually around plus or minus three sigma of the global distribution.
They're named by NMOS first and PMOS second, each one slow, typical, or fast. So TT is typical-typical, SS is slow NMOS and slow PMOS, FF is fast-fast.
Then there are the skewed corners: FS is fast NMOS with slow PMOS, and SF is the reverse.
NMOS and PMOS are built with different process steps, so they can drift in opposite directions. We use them because different checks have different worst cases.
Setup timing, the max-delay check, fails on slow silicon, so we use SS at low voltage and appropriate temperature.
Hold timing fails when things are too fast, so FF at high voltage. Leakage power is worst in FF at high temperature, because fast devices have low threshold and leak.

The skewed corners matter for circuits where the NMOS to PMOS balance is important: SRAM read and write margins, ratioed or pass-gate logic, the switching threshold of inverters, clock duty cycle, and analog biasing.
Each corner is combined with voltage and temperature, like SS at 0. 81 volts and 125 C.
And corners only cover global variation, so I'd add Monte Carlo or on-chip variation derates for local mismatch."
